plan: Eight new SAT R&W items written to a stricter hard-item design: every distractor is partly supported by the text (true-but-incomplete, overreading of a real phrase, or near-miss nuance), with denser academic passages: reductive (WIC), perch-plot seed limitation, Kwan on printing and spelling (qualified response), two-part fertilizer data, function of a both-views-predict sentence, colon versus such-as, past counterfactual, Jevons paradox synthesis. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: An austere poet
passages.text: Critics often call the poet's late work austere, but the label is somewhat ______: although her diction in these poems is indeed spare, the poems themselves are dense with allusions to scripture, folk song, and her own earlier work, and they reward patient rereading.

passages.title: Perches and shrubs
passages.text: Birds deposit most of the seeds they eat beneath the places where they perch, so plants whose seeds are spread by birds often grow in clusters around trees and fences. In a restored grassland, ecologists installed artificial perches in some plots and left others without perches. After three years, shrubs spread by birds had become established in the perch plots at five times their density in the other plots, while plants spread by wind showed no difference between the two kinds of plots. These results suggest that, in this grassland, the establishment of bird-spread shrubs had been limited mainly by ______

passages.title: Printing and spelling
passages.text:
Text 1
Many historians have credited the printing press with rapidly standardizing English spelling. Once texts could be reproduced in thousands of identical copies, they argue, printers quickly settled on uniform spellings that readers then absorbed.

Text 2
Historian Ada Kwan examined books printed in London between 1500 and 1650 and found that spellings varied widely, even among books from the same print shop and sometimes on the same page. Kwan does not deny that printing contributed to standard spelling, but she argues that uniform spelling took hold only gradually, after dictionaries and schoolbooks spread fixed forms in the late 1600s and 1700s.

passages.title: Fertilizer in dry years
passages.text:
Researchers tested a new fertilizer on wheat in a dry year and a wet year.
Dry year: 2.0 tonnes per hectare without fertilizer; 2.6 with fertilizer.
Wet year: 3.5 tonnes per hectare without fertilizer; 3.8 with fertilizer.
The researchers claim that the fertilizer's benefit was greater in the dry year, whether measured in tonnes or as a percentage of the unfertilized yield.

passages.title: Discovered or invented?
passages.text: Philosophers have long debated whether moral principles are discovered, like facts about the physical world, or invented, like the rules of a game. Defenders of discovery often point to the striking similarities among the moral codes of societies that had no contact with one another. Yet such similarities are also what the invention view would predict if those codes arose as solutions to problems that every society faces, such as dividing food and settling disputes. The similarities alone, then, cannot settle the question.

passages.title: Expedition supplies
passages.text: To keep their sleds light on the long crossing of the ice sheet, the team carried only three ______ water, a compass, and a satellite radio.

passages.title: A costly flaw
passages.text: If the engineers ______ the flaw in the bridge's design sooner, the structure would not have needed the costly repairs that closed it for most of last year.

passages.title: Jevons's coal question
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons studied Britain's use of coal.
- Steam engines had become far more efficient, using less coal for the same work.
- Jevons observed that Britain's total coal use had risen rather than fallen.
- More efficient engines made coal-powered work cheaper.
- Cheaper coal-powered work led people to use coal for many more tasks.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: although her diction in these poems is indeed spare
candidates.explanation: The text grants that the diction is spare (so the label is partly right) but says the label misses the poems' richness. A label that oversimplifies by capturing only one feature is "reductive."

A.rationale: "Redundant" would mean the label repeats something already said; the text's point is that the label captures only part of the poems.

B.rationale: The label is not unclear in meaning; the problem is that it leaves out the poems' density.

D.rationale: Nothing concerns whether the label is new.

hints: Does the text say the label is wrong, or that it leaves something out?

strategy.explanation: Predict "too simple" before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: When a text concedes part of a claim, look for a word meaning "incomplete," not "false."

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: how many of their seeds reached a given plot.
choices.B: how well their seedlings could grow once seeds had arrived.
choices.C: competition from the plants whose seeds are spread by wind.
choices.D: how many birds were living in the grassland as a whole.

candidates.evidence: while plants spread by wind showed no difference
candidates.explanation: Perches change where bird-spread seeds land. Shrubs multiplied only where perches brought seeds, and wind-spread plants, whose seed arrival was unchanged, did not differ, so seed arrival was the limiting factor.

B.rationale: If growing conditions were the limit, adding perches, which brings seeds, would not have multiplied shrub density.

C.rationale: Wind-spread plants did not differ between plots, so a change in competition does not explain the shrubs' increase.

D.rationale: Perches redirect where birds drop seeds within the grassland; the result concerns which plots seeds reached, not the total number of birds.

hints: What did the perches change, and what did they leave the same?

strategy.explanation: Use the wind-spread plants as the comparison.

candidates.remember: When only one factor changes and one group responds, that factor was what limited it.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Kwan (Text 2) most likely respond to the historians' view in Text 1?

choices.A: She would argue that the printing press had no meaningful effect on the way English words were spelled.
choices.B: She would agree that printers settled on uniform spellings quickly and then spread them to readers.
choices.C: She would argue that English spelling had already become standardized before the printing press arrived.
choices.D: She would grant printing a role but argue standardization was slower and depended on later developments.

candidates.evidence: Kwan does not deny that printing contributed to standard spelling
candidates.explanation: Kwan accepts that printing contributed but says standard spelling came gradually, with dictionaries and schoolbooks, so she would dispute the speed and the sole credit Text 1 gives printing.

A.rationale: Kwan explicitly does not deny that printing contributed to standard spelling.

B.rationale: Her evidence shows spellings varied widely in printed books, even within one shop.

C.rationale: She places standardization after printing, in the late 1600s and 1700s, not before it.

hints: What does Kwan grant, and what does she dispute?

strategy.explanation: Separate the concession from the objection.

candidates.remember: A response that concedes one point and disputes another is a qualification, not a rejection.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the researchers' claim?

choices.A: Fertilized wheat yielded 3.8 tonnes per hectare in the wet year but only 2.6 tonnes in the dry year.
choices.B: Fertilizer added 0.6 tonnes (30 percent) in the dry year but 0.3 tonnes (about 9 percent) in the wet.
choices.C: In the dry year, fertilizer raised the yield by 0.6 tonnes, from 2.0 to 2.6 tonnes per hectare.
choices.D: Fertilizer added 0.6 tonnes in the dry year and 0.3 tonnes in the wet year, twice as much in tonnes.

candidates.evidence: whether measured in tonnes or as a percentage of the unfertilized yield
candidates.explanation: The claim has two parts. Only B shows the dry-year benefit is larger in tonnes (0.6 versus 0.3) and as a percentage (0.6/2.0 = 30 percent versus 0.3/3.5, about 9 percent).

A.rationale: This compares fertilized yields across years, not the fertilizer's added benefit in each year.

C.rationale: This gives the dry-year benefit only, with no comparison to the wet year or any percentage.

D.rationale: This covers the benefit in tonnes but not the percentage part of the claim.

hints: How many parts does the claim have?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both measures.

candidates.remember: A claim with "whether ... or ..." needs evidence for both measures.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It offers new evidence that moral principles were invented rather than discovered.
choices.B: It explains why separate societies developed moral codes that differ from one another.
choices.C: It argues that evidence cited for one view fits the opposing view equally well.
choices.D: It concedes that the discovery view correctly explains where moral principles come from.

candidates.evidence: such similarities are also what the invention view would predict
candidates.explanation: The defenders of discovery cite similar moral codes; the third sentence shows the invention view predicts the same similarities, so the evidence fits both, which the last sentence states.

A.rationale: The sentence presents no new evidence; it reinterprets the same similarities.

B.rationale: The sentence concerns why codes are similar, not why they differ.

D.rationale: "Yet" signals a challenge to the discovery view's evidence, not a concession to it.

hints: What does "also" tell you about the evidence?

strategy.explanation: Ask how the third sentence treats the evidence from the second.

candidates.remember: Evidence that both sides predict cannot decide between them.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The independent clause "the team carried only three essentials" is complete, so a colon can introduce the list that names them.

B.rationale: A colon should not follow "such as," because "such as" already introduces the list.

C.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but the list is not one.

D.rationale: This creates a comma splice: "these were water ..." is an independent clause.

hints: Is the part before the blank a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check what can introduce a list after a complete clause.

candidates.remember: Use a colon to introduce a list after a complete clause, never after "such as."

candidates.subskill: Verb tense in a past counterfactual
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The sentence describes an unreal past condition (they did not notice sooner). The if-clause takes the past perfect, "had noticed," paired with "would not have needed."

A.rationale: In Standard English, "would have" belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause.

B.rationale: The present perfect does not fit a condition about the past that did not happen.

C.rationale: The future tense cannot describe a past condition.

hints: Did the engineers notice the flaw sooner?

strategy.explanation: Match the if-clause to "would not have needed."

candidates.remember: Past unreal conditions pair "had" + past participle with "would have."

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why Jevons's observation seemed surprising and how it can be explained. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 1865, Jevons observed that Britain's total coal use had risen even as its steam engines became more efficient.
choices.B: Engines used less coal per task, yet coal use rose, since cheaper coal power led people to use it more.
choices.C: More efficient engines made coal-powered work cheaper, which led people to use coal for many more tasks.
choices.D: The economist William Stanley Jevons studied Britain's use of coal in 1865, when steam engines were improving.

candidates.evidence: Jevons observed that Britain's total coal use had risen rather than fallen.
candidates.explanation: Only B states the surprise (more efficient engines, yet more coal used) and the explanation (cheaper coal power encouraged many more uses).

A.rationale: This presents the surprising observation but does not explain it.

C.rationale: This gives the explanation but never says what was surprising about the outcome.

D.rationale: This introduces Jevons and his topic but gives neither the surprise nor the explanation.

hints: Which choice does both things the goal names?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for the surprise and the explanation.

candidates.remember: A two-part goal needs both parts in the answer.
